title: 2027 Medicare Advantage Cuts: Is Your Plan Affected?

sections.text: What's Happening With Medicare Advantage Plans in 2027

sections.content: Several major insurers are reducing the number of Medicare Advantage plans they offer or leaving certain counties entirely for 2027. If you have Medicare Advantage, this doesn't change your Original Medicare benefits, which stay the same regardless of which private plans are available where you live.

What it does mean is that your current plan may not be offered when the next Annual Election Period arrives this fall. Some members will get a notice that their plan is ending, while others will simply find fewer options to choose from when comparing coverage for next year.

This article walks through how to check whether your plan is affected, what your options are if it's being discontinued, and how to compare plans during the Annual Election Period without feeling rushed.

sections.text: Why Insurers Are Scaling Back Medicare Advantage Offerings

sections.content: Insurers are facing a mix of rising medical costs and tighter federal reimbursement rates, which squeezes the profit margins on many Medicare Advantage plans. Rather than absorb those costs across every plan option, some carriers are narrowing their offerings, especially in counties where they previously sold many similar plans.

In practical terms, this often means consolidation. A carrier that once offered five overlapping plans in your county might now offer two, combining benefits rather than spreading them thin. Fewer choices on paper doesn't automatically mean worse coverage, but it does mean you'll want to look closely at what's changed in the plan that remains.

This shift is an industry-wide trend driven by cost pressures and payment policy, not a reflection of your health history or how you've used your benefits. Carriers make these decisions at the plan and county level, based on business factors unrelated to individual members.

sections.text: How to Check If Your Plan Is Affected

sections.content: The clearest signal comes from your Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) letter, which carriers mail each September. This letter outlines any changes to your plan's costs, benefits, and service area for the coming year, and it will state directly if your plan is not being renewed.

items: Read your ANOC letter in full when it arrives in September, not just the summary page.
Look specifically for a non-renewal or termination notice from your carrier.
Confirm your plan's service area still includes your county for 2027.
Call your plan's member services line directly to verify your plan's active status.
Log into your Medicare account at Medicare.gov to check your current plan details.

sections.calloutText: You can confirm whether your plan is still active in your area by checking your Medicare account or calling 1-800-MEDICARE, in addition to contacting your carrier directly.

sections.text: What Happens If Your Plan Is Discontinued

sections.content: If your Medicare Advantage plan is non-renewed, you will not lose Medicare coverage altogether. You still have Original Medicare as a foundation, and you'll have the opportunity to enroll in a new plan. What matters is taking action within the right window so your coverage continues without a gap.

Members whose plans are non-renewed typically qualify for a [Special Enrollment Period](https://www.medicare.gov/) that allows them to pick a new Medicare Advantage plan or return to Original Medicare outside the standard Annual Election Period. Carriers are required to notify affected members in advance, giving you time to compare new options before your current plan ends.

If you do nothing, you may be defaulted into a different plan chosen by your carrier or left with gaps in prescription or supplemental coverage you were counting on. A default plan rarely matches your specific doctors, medications, or budget, so reviewing your options yourself, even briefly, is worth the time.

sections.text: Choosing a New Plan During the Annual Election Period

sections.content: The [Annual Election Period runs from October 15 to December 7](https://www.medicare.gov/), giving every Medicare Advantage member a defined window to compare plans and make a change for the following year. Changes made during this period take effect January 1.

Start by listing your current doctors, specialists, and prescriptions. This list becomes your reference point for checking whether a new plan's network includes your providers and whether its formulary covers your medications at a cost you can manage.

Compare total costs rather than just the monthly premium. Look at copays for specialist visits, deductibles, and the plan's maximum out-of-pocket limit, which is capped at $9,250 for in-network services in 2026 for Medicare Advantage plans, though this figure can shift from year to year. A plan with a low premium can still cost more overall if your copays and drug costs are higher.

This is also a good moment to ask whether Medicare Advantage still fits your situation, or whether Original Medicare paired with a [Medicare Supplement plan](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) and a standalone Part D plan might serve you better this year, particularly if your health needs or travel patterns have changed.

Before you compare any new plan, pull together your medication list with exact dosages and your doctors' names and specialties. I've found that having this ready before you call anyone, whether it's the carrier or a licensed agent, saves time and leads to a more accurate comparison instead of a generic recommendation.

sections.text: Avoiding Common Mistakes When Switching Plans

sections.content: Waiting until the final week of AEP is one of the most common mistakes. When you compress your research into just a few days, you lose the chance to call plans, confirm network details, and think through your decision without pressure.

items: Choosing a plan based on a low premium alone without checking how your specific prescriptions are covered.
Assuming your doctor is still in-network because they were last year, instead of calling the doctor's office directly to confirm.
Overlooking the plan's drug formulary tier placement, which affects your actual copay at the pharmacy.
Missing the December 7 deadline, which can leave you without the ability to change plans until the next enrollment period.

sections.calloutText: If you miss the December 7 deadline and don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you typically have to wait for the next enrollment window, which could mean staying in a plan that no longer fits your needs for an entire year.

sections.content: You're allowed to take your time reviewing your options before you speak with anyone. Reading your ANOC letter, checking your plan's network, and comparing a few alternatives on your own first is a reasonable way to approach this.

When you're ready, a licensed Medicare agent can review your doctors, prescriptions, and budget with you and explain how different plans compare, without requiring you to decide on the spot. Honest guidance sounds like an agent answering your specific questions and pointing out tradeoffs; a pressured pitch sounds like being pushed toward one plan before your questions are answered.
Before sharing personal information with anyone, confirm they are a licensed agent and ask how they are compensated. A trustworthy source will answer directly and won't rush you off the phone.

faqs.question: How do I know if I need to act right away or if I have more time?
faqs.answer: Your ANOC letter arrives in September and tells you whether your plan is changing or ending. The Annual Election Period then runs October 15 to December 7, giving you weeks to compare options. Reviewing your ANOC as soon as it arrives gives you plenty of time before the deadline.

faqs.question: Will I be pressured into a decision if I call for help?
faqs.answer: No. Licensed Medicare agents are there to explain your options based on your doctors, prescriptions, and budget, not to push you toward a sale. You can ask as many questions as you need, take notes, and end the call at any time without making a decision.

faqs.question: Can I just research this on my own first?
faqs.answer: Yes, reading your ANOC letter and comparing plans independently is a reasonable first step. If you'd like a second opinion afterward, a licensed agent can review your choice with you at no cost before you enroll.

faqs.question: How can I trust that the information I find online is accurate?
faqs.answer: Rely on official sources like your ANOC letter, your Medicare account at Medicare.gov, and licensed agents who can confirm current details. If something you read seems inconsistent with your plan, verify it directly with your carrier or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE.

sections.text: Next Steps: Review Your Plan Before AEP Begins

sections.content: Start by reading your ANOC letter closely, confirming your plan's network still covers your county, and comparing total costs across a few alternatives rather than just premiums. These few steps give you a clear picture of where you stand before the Annual Election Period gets busy.

Reviewing your options early, rather than waiting for the December 7 deadline, gives you room to ask questions and compare calmly. If you'd like a second set of eyes on your comparison, a licensed agent can walk through it with you without any pressure to enroll on the spot.
